question: What are the main caching patterns with Redis and what are their trade-offs?
title: Redis Caching Patterns
direct_answer: Cache-aside (lazy loading): app checks cache first, queries DB on miss, writes to cache. Simple but can have stale data until TTL expires. Write-through: write to cache AND DB on every update — always consistent but higher write latency. Write-behind (write-back): write to cache immediately, persist to DB asynchronously — fast writes but risk of data loss on cache crash. Read-through: cache fetches from DB automatically on miss. For most web apps, cache-aside with TTL is the right default.
interviewer_intent: Tests caching strategy knowledge beyond just 'use Redis'. Trade-offs matter.

sections.title: Caching pattern comparison
sections.content:
Cache-aside (Lazy Loading): application code checks Redis first. Cache hit: return cached. Cache miss: fetch from DB, store in Redis with TTL, return. The cache is populated on demand. Stale data possible until TTL expires. Extra DB load on cold start.

Write-through: on every DB write, also write to cache. Cache is always fresh. Higher write latency (two writes per mutation). Cache may contain objects that are never read (wasted memory).

Write-behind: write to cache immediately, return to caller, persist to DB in background. Fastest writes. Risk of data loss if Redis crashes before DB write. Complex error handling. Use only for analytics counters and other append-only patterns.

Cache invalidation strategies: TTL (simplest, eventually consistent), event-based (delete/update cache on model change), version tags (include a version key in cache keys, increment to invalidate group).

sections.title: Cache-aside implementation
sections.content:
import json
import redis.asyncio as aioredis
from functools import wraps
from typing import Callable, TypeVar, ParamSpec

r = aioredis.from_url('redis://localhost')

# Cache-aside helper
async def get_cached(key: str, fetch_fn: Callable, ttl: int = 300):
    cached = await r.get(key)
    if cached:
        return json.loads(cached)
    result = await fetch_fn()
    await r.setex(key, ttl, json.dumps(result))
    return result

# Usage
async def get_user(user_id: int, db: AsyncSession) -> dict:
    key = f'user:{user_id}'
    async def fetch():
        user = await db.get(User, user_id)
        return {'id': user.id, 'email': user.email}
    return await get_cached(key, fetch, ttl=3600)

# Cache invalidation on update
async def update_user_email(user_id: int, email: str, db: AsyncSession) -> None:
    user = await db.get(User, user_id)
    user.email = email
    await db.commit()
    await r.delete(f'user:{user_id}')  # invalidate cache

# Write-through
async def update_user_write_through(user_id: int, email: str, db: AsyncSession) -> dict:
    user = await db.get(User, user_id)
    user.email = email
    await db.commit()
    updated = {'id': user_id, 'email': email}
    await r.setex(f'user:{user_id}', 3600, json.dumps(updated))  # keep in sync
    return updated

seo.metaTitle: Redis Caching Patterns — Cache-Aside, Write-Through, Cache Invalidation
seo.metaDescription: Redis caching strategies: cache-aside lazy loading, write-through consistency, write-behind performance, and cache invalidation on update.

speakable_v2.hook: Cache-aside with TTL is the right default for 90% of web apps — simple, works, and eventual staleness is usually acceptable.

beats.content: Check Redis first. Cache hit: return. Cache miss: query DB, store in Redis with TTL, return. Populated on demand. The risk: stale data between writes and TTL expiry.
Write-through keeps cache in sync: every DB write also updates the cache. Always fresh, but higher write latency and you cache things that may never be read.
On update, delete the cache key immediately. The next read will be a cache miss, fetching fresh from DB. Simpler than write-through for most cases.

speakable_v2.cap: Cache stampede: many requests miss the cache simultaneously and all hit the DB at once. Fix with short-lived distributed locks or probabilistic early expiration (Redis 4.0+ LFU policy).
speakable_v2.followup_handoff: Follow up with cache stampede prevention with Redis SETNX locks, or cache key versioning for group invalidation.
